chokhmat-shlomo/4:_: Seif 4 in Hagahah: nevertheless he goes to synagogue to hear Megillah etc. NB I was in doubt regarding a woman — what is her law, whether she is permitted to go to synagogue to hear Megillah. What brought me to this doubt is per what a certain scholar aroused me to explain for him Rashba's responsum general 27 law 2, who wrote: and a mourner does not leave his house's door the first Shabbat to hear blessing of milah and blessing of bridegrooms; and this that is difficult for you, that a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot stated in Torah — this refers to positive mitzvot in his body such as tzitzit and tefillin or to circumcise his son; but to go to milah and canopy and to hear the blessing for the sake of gemilut chasadim he has no permission to leave his house's door — end of his words. [Brought in Shach Yoreh Deah siman 393 see there.] On this the aforementioned scholar asked: from what is written regarding Megillah, explicit here that he is permitted to go hear Megillah — per the questioner's words now. Behold at first glance it appeared to me to settle that Rashba's intent is specifically where the mitzvah is in action, such as putting on tefillin and the like — then he is permitted to go even though he nullifies mourning, since mourning is all its prohibition in shev v'lo taaseh d'rabbanan, and behold for a Torah prohibition too a positive mitzvah overrides a negative — all the more for d'rabbanan of action which is stronger; unlike hearing blessings and the like which are not action in his body — therefore anything without action in a Torah prohibition is not overridden, and the same for d'rabbanan, for whatever the rabbis enacted they enacted like d'oraisa. Therefore regarding Megillah, since here each is obligated to read Megillah and what one discharges another is by agency, as Peri Megadim wrote in Orach Chayyim and in Sefer Kaf HaChayyim, and I extended on this elsewhere — if so here, since the essence of the mitzvah is obligation on his body in action, only the agent acts and it is as him — if so here there is action, similar to tzitzit and tefillin etc. Per this it appears this is specifically for a male, for the obligation is upon him to read Megillah and what one discharges another is by agency — therefore there is action and mourning is deferred. But for a woman, since she is not obligated in reading only in hearing — if so whoever hears fulfills and she needs no agency at all — here it is like hearing blessings and mourning is not deferred; therefore she is forbidden to go out to hear Megillah since there is no action in her body. So it appeared to him. However in truth there is no proof from this to say one may not learn from Megillah reading because of other things — for behold even Torah study is canceled to hear Megillah reading, and many Torah mitzvot are deferred before Megillah reading; therefore mourning too is deferred before Megillah reading. On the contrary I wonder at those who forbid below in Shulchan Aruch for a mourner to leave his house to hear Megillah; and even those who permit here — nevertheless Rama wrote if possible to gather a minyan at home it is preferable. And why should it be so — behold Torah study, which is stringent, is canceled to hear Megillah reading, and it is clear in poskim that even if possible to read afterward in ten, nevertheless they cancel in order to hear in public. If so, if Torah study which is stringent is canceled, all the more mourning which is lighter; behold this kal vachomer itself they learned in gemara for Torah from avodah: if avodah which is stringent is canceled, Torah which is lighter — not all the more; if so this kal vachomer one may learn all the more regarding mourning which is lighter than Torah and avodah — requires study. Behold in the body of the aforementioned questioner's difficulty on the aforementioned Rashba — from what is written regarding Megillah, in any case it is not difficult, since in Shulchan Aruch there are several views whether a mourner may leave his house — one may say Rashba truly holds he does not leave his house even to hear Megillah. However one who is exacting in Rashba's responsum language will see his intent is thus: the distinction is between whether the essence of the mitzvah depends on his body, such as tzitzit, tefillin, milah where the essence depends on his body — for these we say we defer mourning before them; but a matter not done by him alone only with others' combination, such as hearing milah blessing or canopy blessing — if others were not doing the mitzvah he would have no obligation at all, and the mitzvah is not the essence of his body's obligation, only if others do the mitzvah he too is obligated to go with them to repay kindness — for this we do not defer mourning. If so automatically no question from Megillah, for there whether for men or women the obligation depends on each person's body by himself, either to read Megillah or to hear — therefore we defer mourning before them. Behold what I challenged above — why the mourner does not go hear Megillah from avodah and Torah — here one could say thus per what is written siman 232 and siman 231: one distinguishes between he began in permission and does not stop, and he began in prohibition and stops for all; if so here too what kohanim in their avodah and leviim on the platform cancel their avodah, and likewise the yeshiva of the house of Rabbi — this is when he began on Purim itself at the time the reading obligation already applied to him, therefore they are obligated to cancel; but if he began in permission he does not stop; if so mourning that applied to him before Purim — since this mourning obligation applied before Megillah — he does not stop from mourning to read Megillah. Per this it would appear if mourning did not apply to him except on Purim itself, such as buried on Purim night and the like — then for all he is permitted to go hear Megillah even if he can gather a minyan at home, nevertheless he goes to hear in public, even for those who hold mourning applies on Purim too. So it appeared to me now — requires study. Behold as I speak on this I will mention what arose in my thought to challenge on what we say in gemara there in Megillah: R' Yehoshua ben Levi said a person must read Megillah at night and repeat it by day, as written "so that Your glory may sing and not be silent" etc.; he thought the baraita of daytime helps; a certain rabbi told him etc. like one who passes this portion and teaches it; it is difficult — from R' Yehoshua ben Levi's language it implies his emphasis is on daytime that he is obligated to read also by day; if the emphasis were on night and by day it would be obvious to him — he should have said a person must read Megillah also at night; and since he said a person must read Megillah at night and repeat by day, it implies his main emphasis is on daytime. Difficult on daytime — why did he need the verse "so that Your glory may sing" etc.; and in particular how could he think from it the baraita of daytime, but hold reading obligation is not by day, and how did it enter his mind to say so? Behold since it is written mishpacha u'mishpacha we learn kohanim in their avodah and leviim on the platform and Israel in their maamad cancel their avodah to hear Megillah reading — at night there is no platform and no maamad, per force it deals with daytime reading — if so proven reading is by day. Also from kohanim in their avodah one could challenge: even though burning limbs is valid all night, nevertheless since we wrote it is proven from poskim' words that where another mitzvah applied to him before Megillah it is not deferred before Megillah — if so per force what kohanim cancel in their avodah is by day when this obligation applied to them together with Megillah, unlike burning limbs at night that applied to them from day 13 before Megillah obligation. If so one may learn kal vachomer: if mourning is not deferred before Megillah, all the more avodah which is stringent; per force it does not deal with nighttime when there is no avodah, only what remains of the day; if so per force it deals from daytime — and how could it enter his mind there is no Megillah reading by day — requires study now — requires study well. (there in that seif in Hagahah) And some say mourning does not apply on Purim, neither on the 14th nor on the 15th etc. NB from this I learned another new law regarding shmuah kerovah on Purim that in the end becomes distant — its law as explicit in Shulchan Aruch and in Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah siman 402: shmuah kerovah on Shabbat that in the end becomes distant — he practices only one hour; explicit there in Beit Yosef in name of Rashba's responsum the reason: even though mourning applies on Shabbat and counts even at its beginning — nevertheless here it is different, for mourning does not apply afterward except from Shabbat force while it is still the thirty-day day; if so the secondary should not be more stringent than it, for in it mourning does not apply yet its cause causes mourning — see there; if so here too since on Purim mourning does not apply, the cause should not be more stringent. Per this it appears further: even if Purim occurred after Shabbat and it is the thirty-day day on Purim and he was informed on Shabbat too — he does not have the law of shmuah kerovah, for his law is like hearing inside the festival and after the festival becomes distant. Superficially one could distinguish and say on a festival properly he has the law of distant shmuah, since on a festival mourning did not apply to him, for festival does not count in the seven — if so necessarily now mourning did not apply to him, and after the festival at the hour mourning began on him it was already distant — therefore he has distant shmuah law even though still within the thirty-day day itself. On Shabbat, even though Shabbat counts and mourning applies to him — nevertheless since on Shabbat it deals with the thirty-day day itself, and such since it is the last day and we hold part of the day is like the whole — if so if he already knew the matter mourning was already ceased from him, only that since he still did not know his law is like the day before — therefore enough to be stringent if mourning applied immediately; but if now it is Shabbat and mourning did not apply for all its laws, they were not stringent to be like the day before, and we say in it part of the day is like the whole. But if he was informed on Shabbat that within the thirty days only immediately adjacent to Shabbat is Purim, a festival on which mourning does not apply in eating, and afterward it became distant — here properly he has shmuah kerovah law, since he was informed within thirty days itself and Shabbat counts in the seven — nevertheless per Rashba's responsum reason that the secondary should not be more stringent than itself, it appears there is no distinction in the matter, and in every case mourning ceases from him since afterward it will not apply except from Shabbat force and the secondary will not be more stringent. And truthfully, without Rashba's words it would appear the reason of the matter of shmuah kerovah on Shabbat and after festival becomes distant — he practices only one hour — we were because the reason of shmuah kerovah is the day of hearing is as if before him. Therefore it appears this is specifically on a day that if he died now aninut of the first day would apply, whether before burial or after burial; therefore here it is relevant to say the day of hearing is as if before him. But on Shabbat and festival, if he died for him now aninut law after burial would not apply, as Rashba wrote in Laws of Chol HaMoed: if the first day is on Chol HaMoed he puts on tefillin — even disputants there, it is for another reason, for otherwise Chol HaMoed is not the main time of tefillin; but otherwise they would agree — if so the stringency of day one after burial did not apply to him, therefore when the essence is nullified the secondary is nullified too. But on Purim, since aninut applies to him by law — and even for those who permit meat and wine, this is only from communal positive mitzvah force, but from tefillin certainly exempt on day one even on Purim — since aninut of day one after burial applied to him, the secondary applied too; unlike Shabbat and festival, if tefillin mitzvah were relevant they would put on tefillin and would not be exempt from tefillin law from aninut after burial — if so since stringency of one day applied to him, the secondary applied too. In any case it appears since halacha follows the lenient in mourning, one may rely on Rashba's reason, especially since my ruling does not decide against Rashba's words even as a drop from the sea. Per Rashba's reason, on Purim too it is so like Shabbat; in particular since in Rama's language here Purim is mentioned like Shabbat, and also Beit HaGadol's view that Purim's law is like festivals that interrupt and do not count at all — in this and this certainly woe if his law were like shmuah kerovah on festival that after festival becomes distant that he practices only one day; therefore in this law there is doubt perhaps like Beit HaGadol and Purim's law is like festivals. And if you say not like Beit HaGadol — perhaps like Rashba's reason; if so even if his law is like Shabbat, here it is like distant shmuah law. Therefore one may rely on the halacha as written, especially in mourning d'rabbanan. So it appeared to me clear for the law — requires study well. May God repair breaches with us Israel and swallow death forever and make us rejoice in His salvation; we end with holy Rama's words end of siman 697: good heart, joy always. I present here what I said in my chiddushim on Orach Chayyim year 5549 on what is brought above siman 695: a person must become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know between arur Haman and baruch Mordechai. It appears as a new matter: behold Chazal said per one view that therefore we do not say Hallel on Purim — we do not say song on a miracle outside the land. It appears this is explicit in the words of the psalmist David who said "Who will give from Zion salvation of Israel — Jacob will exult, Israel will rejoice" — behold the essence of song is said on joy, and if there is no joy there is no song; therefore he said "Who will give from Zion salvation of Israel." If salvation were from Zion, meaning Eretz Yisrael, then Jacob would exult, Israel would rejoice; but if salvation is outside the land and not from Zion, Israel has no joy in it and there is no song. Therefore it appears also for the other view that gemara concludes in Arachin that its reading is its Hallel — since they were exiled they returned to the first permission; nevertheless they made a distinction that a miracle of chutz la'aretz and Eretz Yisrael are not equal. Therefore they enacted on Purim feasting and joy in remembrance of feasting first; and on all Yom Tov we find only mitzvah of joy and not feasting — this is like they enacted on Purim to divide honor to Eretz Yisrael in enactment of walled cities as Ran wrote; so they enacted further that all festivals made for Israel in Eretz Yisrael or before their coming to Eretz Yisrael when all lands are equal — joy alone is relevant; but on Purim when they had already merited Eretz Yisrael before, it would be fitting not to rejoice at all on a miracle in chutz la'aretz. Therefore when they enacted joy they enacted feasting first, so joy not be from the miracle alone but also from feasting, as is the way of all who drink — his heart rejoices — and joy also through feasting, to show feasting too causes joy, and we have no complete joy since the miracle was in chutz la'aretz and not of Eretz Yisrael — therefore feasting and afterward joy. From this reason too, though they enacted to read Megillah which is in place of Hallel for us who hold its reading is its Hallel — nevertheless they enacted likewise to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know between arur Haman etc., so he forget to say the song since its reading is its Hallel. If so proven telling the miracle is the Hallel; if so automatically what is said arur Haman and baruch Mordechai is also Hallel and song; therefore obligated to become intoxicated until he does not know between arur Haman etc., so the song not be in his mouth all day and song not be complete, since it is a miracle in chutz la'aretz our joy in it is not complete — therefore song too will not be complete all day, only he forget it; unlike a miracle in Eretz Yisrael of which it is said "When God returns Zion's captivity" — when the miracle is in Eretz Yisrael then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with rinnah all day, and we will not need to drink to forget the song, only "my tongue shall speak Your righteousness all day, Your glory" — and song will be complete. So may it be with God's help, amen, speedily and in our days, and may the redeemer come to Zion speedily in our days, amen and amen.

Those who die in the suburbs of the next year will not send a shipment of dishes and that year in the same fruit sends the poor flesh or farms and not some kind of phenols and anything happy, until here. This means to me, D.R. Rather, they are established that they are prohibited from doing work. From the age of Heaven. B. Dressed:
kaf-hachayyim/2:_: (b) there. Instead of not doing anything wrong. And at night until the hot hawk, Chery even sang, where he did not. Heaven’s word is that of Heaven’s people, who are in Heaven’s Word, is not Heaven’s word:
kaf-hachayyim/3:_: (3) there. One does not do [melacha]. Through a gentile it is permitted. Magen Avraham s.k. 1. Eliyah Rabbah s.k. 1. Even HaEzer s.k. 1. Orach Chayyim s.k. 1. And likewise when he has nothing to eat, it is permitted to do melacha and sew his friend's garments for wages, for all this is joy for him. Even HaEzer there. Mishna Berurah in Sefer HaTzavaot letter 2; and likewise if there is loss in the matter it is permitted, for anything of joy is permitted on Purim. Mateh Zion s.k. 1. Mishna Berurah in Sefer HaTzavaot s.k. 3.
kaf-hachayyim/4:_: (4) One who was building his house before Purim through a gentile — since the matter became known, he should stop on Purim day. Beit Din siman 695. Birkei Yosef s.k. 3. Orach Chayyim there Shaarei Teshuvah s.k. 1. And in Sefer Chok LeYisrael vol. 2 Yoreh Deah in remnants of Orach Chayyim siman 20 he permitted building a shop on the 14th and 15th and acted thus — see there; building a synagogue and a matter of mitzvah is permitted. Rokeach 1:10:1 and in his book Malach siman 31 s.k. 31.
kaf-hachayyim/5:_: (5) there in Hagahah. And nowadays they practiced everywhere not to do. It appears merchandise is permitted since it is joy for him. Taz s.k. 1. And so Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef s.k. 5, except he wrote: even though we liken to it, we do not make an act to permit commerce on Purim in a place that practiced not to do melacha — but if one transgressed and did, bet din does not fine him unless they made a fence lest people breach in doing melacha; all this depends on the appearance to bet din's eyes — see there. And so Shulchan Gavoah s.k. 3; it appears if bet din sent to warn him not to trade and he did not heed, bet din may put him in nidui. Rokeach s.k. 2; see above siman 554 seif 22 and in our words there b'siyata dishmaya.
kaf-hachayyim/6:_: (b) there. And he does not see Heaven’s blessing, and so on, he will not see Heaven’s blessing. And so he was in his name in the light of his name. But in B.D., it means that we should not do it. From A Scandal:
kaf-hachayyim/7:_: (7) there. He does not see a sign of blessing etc. — it implies a sign of blessing is what is not fitting; behold we call him and do not put him in cherem for him; and so is the view of most poskim; but Rav Acha Gaon in Sheiltot — Hagahot Maimoniot and Razah in Sefer HaMaor and in Orach Chayyim wrote we put him in cherem. Birkei Yosef s.k. 5. Orach Chayyim s.k. 2. For the matter of practice he agreed in Knesset HaGedolah (in Hagahot Beit Yosef end s.k. 2) that nowadays they practiced everywhere not to do, and if one did they do not put him in cherem and do not fine him, only he does not see a sign of blessing. Shulchan Gavoah s.k. 4.
kaf-hachayyim/8:_: (8) It appears to me that even for a Jew they fine only one who does melacha b'mezid; but b'shogeg when he thought melacha was permitted they do not punish him, for shogeg is not like mezid. Knesset HaGedolah there s.k. 3. And if he is b'mezid, even though they do not put him in nidui since it is doubtful in the dispute of poskim — nevertheless they may fine him, for all he profited from that melacha he gives to the poor, all per the judge's view. Rokeach s.k. 3. And so in his book Malach siman 31 s.k. 34.

levushei-serad/7:_: s.k. 12 his law is like Shabbat. For the law of portions is like the law of asking peace, and he wrote there on the 14th in s.k. 3 that on Shabbat there are places that permit asking peace of a mourner and there are places that forbid — therefore in places that practiced permission, portions too are permitted — see there; and the same here on Purim, whose law is also like Shabbat regarding mourning: portions are permitted in a place where they practice permission to ask peace on Shabbat, for according to them it is likewise permitted to ask peace on Purim — therefore portions too are permitted. But Taz s.k. 3 understood Rama's intent here on what Rama wrote there in s.k. 2 that nowadays they are lenient in asking peace of a mourner after thirty days and there is no reason for this unless we say the peace we practice is not called asking peace as in their days — see there; therefore Taz was puzzled on portions, there is no such permission — therefore he wrote one should not rely on this etc.; but per Magen Avraham's explanation there is no difficulty, for Rama's intent is to permit portions on Purim in places that permit on Shabbat asking peace of a mourner, for he holds that even asking peace as in their days was permitted on Shabbat — simple.
levushei-serad/8:_: Magen Avraham s.k. 13 as written siman 688 seif 3. For individual d'oraisa positive mitzvah, namely mourning day one, overrides communal d'rabbanan positive mitzvah, namely joy of two festival days — if so, here too aninut to forbid meat and wine is d'rabbanan and is deferred before Purim which is d'oraisa positive mitzvah; and all the more since it is also communal positive mitzvah — therefore one need not give the reason that mourning is individual positive mitzvah.
